ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The figure shows a bias circuit powered by positive and negative power supplies, with 12 V labeled at the top and -12 V labeled at the bottom. On the left there is a transistor branch, connected through a resistor to +12 V, and the current is labeled 1 mA; the bases of the left transistor and the right transistor are connected, indicating that matched transistors are used to form a reference relationship. The upper side of the right transistor is connected to a differential amplifier module labeled Differential Amplifier, the branch current is labeled 1 μA, and the lower side of the right transistor is connected through resistor R to -12 V. Reasoning: Treating this as matched BJTs with negligible base current, the left transistor sets the collector current IC1 = 1 mA, and the right transistor needs to provide IC2 = 1 μA. The two transistors have the same base, the emitter of the left transistor is directly referenced to -12 V, while the emitter of the right transistor goes through resistor R to -12 V, so the voltage across the right-side emitter resistor is IC2 R. This voltage is equal to the VBE by which the right transistor is reduced relative to the left transistor: IC2 R = VBE1 - VBE2. For matched BJTs, VBE1 - VBE2 = VT ln(IC1/IC2). Substituting VT = 25 mV and IC1/IC2 = 1 mA / 1 μA = 1000 gives R = 25 mV × ln(1000) / 1 μA = 0.025 × 6.9078 / 10^-6 Ω = 172693 Ω = 172.7 kΩ.
